Chevron's FY2025 10-K describes a strategy to "leverage our strengths to safely deliver lower carbon energy to a growing world," with objectives to "lower the carbon intensity of operations and grow new energies businesses [1]." The company's New Energies organization is focused on hydrogen and its derivatives, carbon capture and storage, power generation for data centers, enhanced geothermal, and lithium extraction, and in 2025 hydrogen was produced and introduced into a salt cavern for storage at the ACES Delta site in Utah [2][3]. The company also holds operated and nonoperated working interests in five greenhouse gas assessment permits totaling nearly 10.2 million gross acres to evaluate carbon dioxide storage potential off Australia [4].

At the same time, the 10-K makes clear that growing hydrocarbons remains a core investment priority: the stated strategy explicitly includes an aim to "grow our oil and gas business," and worldwide oil-equivalent production reached 3.7 million barrels per day in 2025, up approximately 12 percent from 2024, driven in part by the Hess acquisition, the completion of the Future Growth Project at Tengizchevroil, and record Permian Basin production [1][5]. The TCO Future Growth Project alone increased crude oil production by 260,000 barrels per day, bringing total gross output to one million barrels of oil-equivalent per day [6]. The filing also notes that some investors have "divergent and evolving views" on the company's ESG-related strategies, "calling for focus on increased production of oil and gas products rather than lower carbon business lines and climate-related targets [7]."

On the regulatory risk side, the 10-K warns that GHG-related legislation, regulation, and government actions "could reduce demand for Chevron's hydrocarbon and other products and/or continue to increase Chevron's operational costs and reduce its return on investment," and that such measures could in some cases "render the extraction of the company's hydrocarbon resources economically infeasible [8]." The filing further states that GHG regulation may result in "increased and substantial capital, compliance, operating, and maintenance costs" and could reduce demand for hydrocarbons, make the company's products more expensive, and adversely affect the economic feasibility of the company's resources [9]. Chevron also identifies risks from stakeholder ESG pressure, noting that unfavorable ESG ratings and divestment initiatives "may lead to negative investor sentiment toward Chevron" and could have a "negative impact on our stock price and our access to and costs of capital [10]."

Regarding the lower-carbon ambitions themselves, the 10-K acknowledges that Chevron has "changed and/or eliminated some of these aspirations, targets, and other ambitions and may continue to do so in the future" for reasons including market conditions, strategy, and financial, operational, and legal factors [10]. The filing identifies numerous contingencies outside Chevron's control that bear on achieving any lower-carbon ambition, including the pace of commercially viable technology, government permitting and incentives, and the availability of cost-effective carbon offsets [10]. Achievement of climate-related initiatives "has, and may continue to, increase costs" and may require purchase of carbon credits or "limit or impact the company's business plans, operations and financial results," while failure to pursue such ambitions could expose the company to government enforcement actions and private litigation [11].
